routes.label: Compare the probabilities and check small values

question: An unfair coin lands on heads with a probability of \(\dfrac14.\) When tossed \(n\) times, the probability of exactly two heads is the same as the probability of exactly three heads. What is the value of \(n?\)
solution:
We must consider both possible head counts and cases where the two events are impossible. Using the usual assumption that successive coin tosses are independent, first suppose \(n\ge3\), so both probabilities are positive.

Let \(P_2\) and \(P_3\) be the probabilities of exactly two and exactly three heads. Choosing the head positions counts each qualifying sequence once. Each sequence with \(k\) heads has probability \((1/4)^k(3/4)^{n-k}\), so
\[
P_2=\binom n2\left(\frac14\right)^2
\left(\frac34\right)^{n-2},
\]
\[
P_3=\binom n3\left(\frac14\right)^3
\left(\frac34\right)^{n-3}.
\]
Because \(P_2>0\), equality is equivalent to \(P_3/P_2=1\). Using \(\binom n2=n(n-1)/2\) and \(\binom n3=n(n-1)(n-2)/6\), we obtain
\[
\frac{P_3}{P_2}
=\frac{n-2}{3}\cdot\frac{1/4}{3/4}
=\frac{n-2}{9}.
\]
Thus \(n-2=9\), giving \(n=11\).

For \(n=1\), neither two nor three heads can occur, so both probabilities are zero and are equal. The same holds for \(n=0\) if zero tosses are allowed. For \(n=2\), the probabilities are \(1/16\) and \(0\), so equality fails.

Therefore the positive-integer solutions are \(1\) and \(11\). Among the listed choices, only \(11\), choice \(\mathrm{D}\), works. It is the unique answer if \(n\ge3\) or if both event probabilities are required to be positive.
